A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEDTOK, and all pages, including Appendices A–C, are readable. Methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched across versions. Revised QA settings require separate treatment of those results but do not prevent a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original EHR prediction experiments in Tables 3–4, modality and codebook-size analyses, and LLaMA3.1-8B medical-QA results.

after.justification: v3 retains the original EHR experiments and reports additional loss ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, medical-QA comparisons and a token-interpretability case study.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the stated straight-through gradient update and moves alpha's weighting from the codebook term to the encoder commitment term. Cross-attention projections become explicitly modality-specific. The dual encoders, partitioned codebook, top-K quantization and token-packing framework remain. These are localized changes to the specified computation; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns of retained experiments.

E1.justification: Medical QA expands from MedDDx-only training and evaluation to MedMCQA training and evaluation on MMLU, MedDDx and AfrimedQA. This substantially broadens the QA data coverage. The three EHR datasets and the corpus of 617,490 codes from eight coding systems remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The medical-QA comparison expands from LLaMA3.1-8B alone to LLaMA3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and MMedLM, each evaluated without and with MEDTOK in Figure 6. This substantially broadens the previously single-model comparison. The five EHR baselines and BERT/VQGraph tokenizer comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The QA protocol changes from fine-tuning on 617 MedDDx-Intermediate questions and testing on 158 Basic and 227 Expert questions to MedMCQA fine-tuning followed by three-benchmark evaluation. New analyses also introduce retraining under four loss configurations and a sweep of equal lambda/beta weights. Existing EHR task definitions, metrics and Appendix B training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds loss-component ablations testing shared and modality-specific optimization separately and together (Table 5), loss-weight sensitivity (Figure 5A), and a frequent-token case study for patients predicted at high risk of hyperlipidemia (Section 4.6). The modality-removal analysis remains, while the existing codebook-size analysis is revised.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 retains three differently seeded ETHOS models and five repeated inference executions. Tables 3–4 retain their parenthesized variability values and reporting format. No new confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 and Figure 4 are unchanged, but v3 adds loss-ablation results and nine LLM–QA-dataset comparisons, replacing the separate Basic/Expert QA results under different training conditions. Codebook-size curves change, including the stated EHRShot optimum from 21,000 to 24,000. Section 4.2 corrects mortality improvement from 11.30% to 11.32% and replaces the Acute MI 8.80% statement with Hyperlipidemia 6.00%, matching unchanged Table 4. The revised QA scores are not same-setting performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: Equations 1–2 replace common d-by-d projection matrices with modality-specific matrices having dimensions compatible with the text and graph embeddings. The straight-through and codebook-loss expressions are also revised. These are limited mathematical corrections; the mutual-information objectives in Equations 6–9 and Appendix C task definitions remain, with no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: unified text-and-graph medical-code tokenization, cross-system generalization, and applicability to EHR models and medical QA. Additional experiments support these existing claims. The small abstract percentage correction does not materially change their scope.

C2.justification: Section 4.6 newly interprets frequent token-to-code mappings as evidence that MEDTOK captures clinically relevant concepts supporting hyperlipidemia prediction. The expanded analyses add interpretations of shared/specific optimization and setting-dependent hyperparameter choices. Existing modality-complementarity and longitudinal-history explanations remain, without a substantive new limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v3 supplies recommended lambda=beta values of 0.1 for inpatient and 0.01 for outpatient settings and replaces the anonymous code-access link with a named GitHub repository. Appendix C explicitly states the final 24 diagnosis codes, consistent with v1's main text. Core hardware, software and training details remain; the revised QA experiment no longer provides the explicit sample counts given in v1.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations for the additional QA datasets and models and for previously used resources including UMLS, MONDO and DrugBank. It also corrects RAW-EHR to RAM-EHR and adds retrieved-knowledge summarization to its description. The main positioning relative to vector-quantized tokenizers and structured EHR models remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Editing concentrates on the method explanations, terminology, captions and appendix headings. Hyperparameter sensitivity receives a separate subsection, QA is renumbered, and an interpretability subsection is added. Publication metadata and a conflict-of-interest statement are updated. The overall narrative structure and most introductory, related-work and concluding text remain.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are substantially revised: v3 adds Table 5, rebuilds Figure 5 around loss-weight and codebook-size sensitivity, replaces the old QA panel with the three-panel Figure 6, and adds the token-frequency Figure 7. Figure 3 is relocated and reduced from full-width to a single-column display. The architecture figures and principal EHR tables are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked controls isolating the shared and modality-specific packing losses and tested QA with only one LLM on one benchmark. v3's Table 5 directly tests those central components across all three EHR datasets, while Figure 6 broadens evidence for QA applicability across three models and benchmarks. Together with the revised training equations and corrected result descriptions, this substantially strengthens the paper's scientific support. New QA sample counts and uncertainty remain unspecified, and changed codebook-sensitivity curves are unexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation.
